description.undefined: A semantic threat ontology and research framework that serves as the ground-truth model for cyber threat intelligence in the CyberTerrain ecosystem. It provides an extensible foundation for modeling cyber threat intelligence concepts, objects, relationships, workflows, and knowledge, and aligns with established CTI framework ontologies — including STONES (STIX 2.1), ATT&CK, CAPEC, CWE, CVE, and CPE — as authoritative reference vocabularies rather than ontologies it imports and extends.

definition.value: An abstract software, hardware, or firmware product line identified by vendor and product name, independent of any specific version or release. Represents the collection of all versioned releases built under that product identity.

scopeNote.value: stonework:Product does not carry version, update, edition, or other release-specific attributes. Those belong on stonework:VersionedProduct. The two classes are disjoint.

comment.en: Instances of stonework:Product represent product families or lines (e.g. 'Apache Log4j', 'Windows 10'). Specific releases are modeled as stonework:VersionedProduct individuals related via stonework:versionOf. CPE entries with wildcard version components map to stonework:Product; entries with concrete versions map to stonework:VersionedProduct.

definition.value: A controlled role type describing the function played by a threat actor within a specific operation, campaign, or criminal organization.

scopeNote.value: A threat actor may play different roles across operations — a nation-state actor may be a sponsor in one campaign and a director in another. Use stonework:RoleAssignment for contextual modeling; stonework:playsRole is the context-free STIX-compatible projection.

definition.value: A threat actor who maintains and operates technical infrastructure during an operation.
A threat actor responsible for designing and building the technical infrastructure supporting operations.
A threat actor who plans and directs operations without necessarily executing them.
A threat actor who executes operations on behalf of a directing or sponsoring entity.
A threat actor who funds or otherwise enables operations without direct participation.
A threat actor who develops malicious code used in operations.

A string identifier transmitted by a client application in HTTP requests declaring the software, version, and platform making the request. Used for fingerprinting clients, identifying malware C2 beaconing patterns, and clustering infrastructure by shared tooling.

scopeNote.value: User-agent strings are observable in network traffic, proxy logs, and web server logs. Distinctive or spoofed user-agent values are commonly used as indicators in threat intelligence. Distinct from stonework:UserAccount (an identity credential) — a UserAgent describes software behavior, not a user identity.

definition.value: Represents a single IP address (IPv4 or IPv6).
A named key in a Windows Registry hierarchy that may contain subordinate keys and registry values.
A prescribed offensive method used by an adversary to achieve a specific tactical objective within a target environment.

scopeNote.value: Aligns with MITRE ATT&CK techniques and D3FEND OffensiveTechnique. The MITRE ATT&CK-shaped realization of stonework:AttackPattern — operationalized for execution, as distinct from CAPEC's more abstract taxonomy-entry shape (capec:AttackPattern, also a stonework:AttackPattern). Framework-specific subclasses (e.g. attack:Technique) provide the concrete individuals. A specific, concrete realization of this technique is modeled as a stonework:Procedure, linked back via stonework:implementedBy.

definition.value: A network-accessible service or endpoint provided by infrastructure, such as HTTP, DNS, or SSH servers.
A specific cyber activity in which a deployed security mechanism changes the security state of one or more cyber entities.

scopeNote.value: Use stonework:madeByActuator for the deployed mechanism, stonework:appliesCountermeasure for the safeguard or procedure being carried out, and stonework:actsOn for each affected entity. Unlike a Countermeasure specification, a SecurityActuation is an occurrence and may carry execution times and produced results. Inspired by SOSA sosa:Actuation without formally importing SOSA.

definition.value: A function, capacity, or part played by an entity in a specific context, relationship, or operation.

scopeNote.value: Roles are typically more stable and relational than Categories. An entity can play multiple Roles. Aligns with patterns in BFO, CCO, and D3FEND (e.g., functional roles of infrastructure or actors).

definition.value: The estimated probability, plausibility, or frequency with which a threat could be realized and lead to a compromise under specified conditions.

scopeNote.value: Likelihood reflects the chance that a compromise will occur, considering adversary capability, intent, opportunity, preconditions, and environmental factors. Likelihood values may be qualitative, ordinal, or quantitative.

comment.undefined: Instances of stonework:Likelihood may incorporate assumptions, uncertainty, adversary behavior, historical frequency, or environmental conditions. Likelihood SHOULD be represented using explicit properties rather than encoded in class IRIs or labels.

definition.value: A classification of an incident's position in the response lifecycle.
The incident has been declared and remains unresolved.
The incident is under active investigation or response.
The incident's spread or immediate harmful activity has been stopped.
Response work is complete and the incident has been formally closed.
A domestic bank account number as issued under a national scheme, without IBAN normalization.

scopeNote.value: The value is stonework:accountNumber. The routing context (US ABA routing number, UK sort code) is recorded on the holding stonework:FinancialInstitution via stonework:abaRoutingNumber or an equivalent, not on this identifier.

definition.value: A physical device that effects a change in a physical process or plant — for example a valve, motor, relay, or servo — as distinct from a cyber security safeguard mechanism.

scopeNote.value: Use for ICS and OT field devices that act on a physical process. Distinct from stonework:SecurityActuator, which is deployed infrastructure that applies a countermeasure. A PLC or motor starter is an Actuator; an EDR agent or firewall is a SecurityActuator. An ICS device that also runs processes and participates in networks may additionally be typed as stonework:Host.

definition.value: An entity that has the capability and intent to conduct harmful activities within a cyber or sociotechnical context.

scopeNote.value: Parent class for stonework:ThreatActorIndividual (a single human) and stonework:ThreatActorGroup (a collective or organization). Threat actors are distinct from the threats they pose; they are the entities that carry out actions that realize threats. They may be linked to observed behaviors, techniques, targeting patterns, and strategic objectives.

definition.value: A documented, structured Behavior that defines a sequenced set of steps, decisions, and actions to be executed in response to a specific type of event, incident, or operational need.

scopeNote.value: A Playbook may be offensive (an adversary's operational playbook — see stonework:OperationPlan) or defensive (an incident response, threat hunting, or recovery playbook) — both are action plans carried out by an interested party, as distinct from stonework:DetectionPlan, which plays a neutral, evaluative role. A Playbook decomposes into Steps via stonework:hasStep; its actual execution is recorded as a stonework:Process.

comment.en: A Playbook is a plan specification; executing one produces instances of stonework:Process. Playbooks are often versioned and tested before use.

definition.value: A Step-decomposed sequence of actions for determining whether observed activity constitutes a security-relevant violation, as distinct from the offensive or defensive action plans that respond to one.

scopeNote.value: A specialization of stonework:InvestigationPlan narrowly scoped to violation triage: orchestrating DetectionRule/Signature evaluation and analytic logic to identify whether a violation occurred, typically triggering a defensive Playbook or ControlPlan via a guarded Transition once one is confirmed. Where a Playbook is an action plan carried out by an interested party — offensive (an adversary's operational playbook) or defensive (an incident responder's playbook) — a DetectionPlan plays a neutral, evaluative role, watching for the kind of changes an InvestigationPlan more broadly investigates.

definition.value: A specific versioned release or build of a Product, identified by a CPE name or equivalent product identifier. Represents the unit of software actually deployed and potentially affected by vulnerabilities.

scopeNote.value: Each CPE 2.3 entry with a concrete version component maps to a stonework:VersionedProduct individual. Wildcard-version CPEs map to stonework:Product. Related to its abstract product line via stonework:versionOf.

comment.en: Instances of stonework:VersionedProduct may include operating systems, applications, libraries, devices, or embedded components at a specific release. Versioning, vendor attribution, and edition details SHOULD be represented using explicit properties rather than encoded strings.

definition.value: A specific installed instance of a VersionedProduct on a particular system or environment, as identified by a SWID tag or equivalent installation record.

scopeNote.value: stonework:ProductInstallation is the intended target for SWID tag data. The installing system, path, licensee, and configuration details belong here rather than on stonework:VersionedProduct.

comment.en: Represents the most granular product identity level: not what software exists, but where and how it is installed. Multiple ProductInstallation individuals may reference the same VersionedProduct.

definition.value: An account that can hold a balance of, or transfer, economic value — fiat currency, cryptocurrency, or monetary-equivalent stored value such as gift-card credit, gaming currency, or loyalty points redeemable for goods.

scopeNote.value: Defined by function, not by the holder: an account at a regulated bank, brokerage, or exchange and a stored-value balance at a non-financial merchant are both FinancialAccounts. Whether it is held at a regulated institution is recorded with the optional stonework:heldAt link, not by the class. Account kind (checking, custodial wallet, prepaid card, exchange account) is asserted with stonework:categorizedBy a stonework:FinancialAccountType. Identifiers such as an IBAN, domestic account number, or crypto address attach with stonework:hasIdentifier. Use stonework:accountCurrency for each currency or crypto asset the account holds or is denominated in; it is intentionally multi-valued. Balance over time is a stonework:MetricObservation. A crypto wallet is a FinancialAccount; its on-chain address is a stonework:CryptoAddress.

definition.value: A free-text annotation attached to one or more individuals to provide additional context, analyst commentary, caveats, or confidence assessments.

scopeNote.value: Notes are analyst-authored rather than machine-generated. They may express uncertainty, sourcing context, or interpretive observations that do not fit structured properties. Corresponds to STIX 2.1 Note SDO.

definition.value: A Playbook specifically representing an adversary's operational plan — the offensive counterpart within the Playbook hierarchy.

scopeNote.value: Named to avoid colliding with the already-established stonework:AttackPattern and stonework:AttackTechnique, and to align with stonework:Operation, whose definition ('a coordinated set of activities... unified command, intent, or resourcing') describes the executed counterpart of an OperationPlan. Generic stonework:Playbook remains available for the undifferentiated or defensive case.

definition.value: A specific method by which adversaries attack AI/ML systems (e.g., training data poisoning, adversarial examples, model extraction).
A structured evaluation of a specific vulnerability's applicability and risk in a particular product or deployment context.

scopeNote.value: Captures VEX-style assessments: whether a product is affected, not affected, fixed, or under investigation, together with the justification and any remediation statement. Distinct from stonework:Vulnerability (which describes the flaw itself) — a VulnerabilityAssessment is an opinion about that flaw in a specific context.

definition.value: A named mutual exclusion object (mutex or semaphore) used by a process to prevent concurrent access to a shared resource. Commonly used as a malware indicator — malware families often create uniquely named mutexes to avoid re-infecting a host.

scopeNote.value: Mutex names serve as host-based indicators of compromise. A specific mutex name found on a system can be attributed to a known malware family. Corresponds to the STIX 2.1 Mutex SCO.

definition.value: A specific occurrence or performance of actions by one or more agents over time within a cyber or sociotechnical context.

scopeNote.value: One of two root classes in STONEWORK alongside CyberEntity. Superclass for Campaigns, CyberActivityClusters, Incidents, Operations, Events, and Processes. Aligns with BFO Occurrent and BFO Process.

definition.value: A single cryptographic hash entry associating a hashing algorithm with its hex-encoded digest value. Used to represent entries in the STIX hashes dictionary.
A defender-owned collection of data or information with organizational value, such as databases, intellectual property, credentials stores, or PII collections.

scopeNote.value: Represents data as a targetable resource distinct from the systems that store or process it. Used to model what adversaries seek to access, exfiltrate, or destroy rather than the infrastructure they exploit to reach it.

definition.value: An abstract malware concept representing a named strain, lineage, or campaign of malicious software sharing common behavioral patterns, code ancestry, or infrastructure. Corresponds to STIX 2.1 malware SDO with is_family=true.

scopeNote.value: Examples: Cobalt Strike, Mimikatz, WannaCry, BlackCat. A MalwareFamily does not have a specific hash or binary but may be linked to MalwareSample instances via the inverse of stonework:memberOfFamily. Use stonework:categorizedBy to assert behavioral type (e.g., stonework:Ransomware, stonework:Backdoor).

definition.value: A type of Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTP) that describes ways that adversaries attempt to compromise targets. Often maps to MITRE ATT&CK techniques.

scopeNote.value: The abstract concept spanning framework-specific shapes that are not structurally identical: CAPEC's shape (capec:AttackPattern) is a taxonomy entry with severity/likelihood/prerequisite fields; MITRE ATT&CK's shape (stonework:AttackTechnique) is an operationalized technique with sub-techniques, procedures, mitigations, and detections. Both are AttackPatterns; stonework:relatedAttackPattern links instances across shapes that describe the same underlying technique.

definition.value: A person who provides information, intelligence, or a report (as opposed to automated feeds or technical artifacts).

scopeNote.value: Often used in HUMINT or OSINT contexts. Reliability scoring is commonly applied to human sources.

definition.value: A classification of a threat actor by their organizational form, affiliation, or primary mode of operation.

scopeNote.value: Applied via stonework:categorizedBy to ThreatActor individuals. A threat actor may have multiple types. Aligns with the STIX 2.1 threat-actor-type open vocabulary.

definition.value: A threat actor motivated by political, social, or ideological causes, using cyber means to advance their agenda.
An individual with technical skills conducting intrusions, ranging from hobbyist to professional.
A government or state-sponsored actor conducting cyber operations for geopolitical objectives.
A threat actor conducting cyber espionage to collect intelligence for a state or organization.
A current or former employee, contractor, or partner acting maliciously due to grievance.
An individual or loosely organized group conducting cyber crimes for personal financial benefit.
A commercial entity conducting cyber espionage or sabotage against business rivals.
A threat actor using cyber means to cause fear, disruption, or harm in support of extremist goals.
An insider who causes harm unintentionally through negligence or error.
An organized criminal group conducting cyber operations for financial gain.
A threat actor motivated primarily by notoriety, publicity, or the thrill of the attack.
A significant urban settlement, municipality, or metropolitan area.
A concrete, observable sequence of actions, commands, or behaviors that implements a technique in a specific operational context.

scopeNote.value: One realization path for a single Technique — the specific commands, scripts, tools, or configuration that carry it out (e.g. the comsvcs.dll MiniDump way of doing OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory). Technique-scoped and typically linear. A Procedure may be only a prose description — the common case when ingesting MITRE ATT&CK procedure examples — or decomposed into stonework:Step individuals via stonework:hasStep for sub-step depth. Links to the Technique it operationalizes via stonework:implements or its specialization stonework:procedureFor. Distinct from stonework:Playbook / stonework:OperationPlan / stonework:ControlPlan, which are objective-scoped plans that orchestrate several Procedures or Techniques with branching, retry, and control flow; a Plan's Step commonly stonework:implements a Procedure.

comment.undefined: Procedures are instances or patterns of execution that realize a technique. They may include command lines, API calls, malware behaviors, or operator playbook steps. Procedures are distinct from techniques, which describe generalized methods.

definition.value: A reference to an external online resource (URL, article, post, etc.) used for provenance.
A classification of the security dimension or consequence affected by an impact.
Impact involving unauthorized alteration or loss of trustworthiness.
Impact involving loss of stakeholder trust or public standing.
Impact involving unauthorized disclosure of information.
Impact involving potential harm to people or physical well-being.
Impact involving direct or indirect monetary loss.
Impact affecting timely and reliable access to systems or information.
A specific, contextualized recommended action or set of steps to prevent or respond to a threat, attack, or incident.

scopeNote.value: More prescriptive and situational than a general Mitigation — a CourseOfAction packages guidance for a specific threat context. Corresponds to the STIX 2.1 CourseOfAction SDO. General reusable controls (e.g. ATT&CK mitigations) are modeled as Mitigation; specific incident response actions are CourseOfAction.

definition.value: A specific branch of economic activity or commercial sector (typically modeled using NAICS or similar codes).

scopeNote.value: Examples: Financial Services, Manufacturing, Retail, Pharmaceuticals.

definition.value: An organization whose business is holding, moving, exchanging, or safeguarding financial assets on behalf of others — a bank, credit union, broker-dealer, payment processor, money services business, or virtual asset service provider.

scopeNote.value: The natural bearer of institution identifiers (stonework:bic, stonework:abaRoutingNumber) that should not broaden bare stonework:Organization, and the range of stonework:heldAt. Institution kind is asserted with stonework:categorizedBy a stonework:FinancialInstitutionType. The Legal Entity Identifier is a general organization identifier (stonework:lei), not institution-specific.

definition.value: A structured list of access control entries (ACEs) that governs which principals (users, groups, or system accounts) are permitted or denied specific operations on a resource.

scopeNote.value: Applies across filesystems, operating system objects (registry keys, processes), network devices (firewall rules), cloud IAM policies, and APIs. In a CTI context, adversaries frequently modify ACLs to establish persistence, escalate privileges, or deny defenders access to compromised resources. Framework-specific extensions (e.g. Windows DACL/SACL structure) are modeled at the framework layer.

definition.value: A unit in which monetary value is denominated — a fiat currency or a crypto asset.

scopeNote.value: The range of stonework:currency on stonework:MonetaryAmount. Fiat units are supplied as a closed controlled vocabulary in stonework:fiatCurrencyScheme (ISO 4217). Crypto units are stonework:CryptoAsset individuals, created as needed rather than pre-enumerated. Currency itself carries no instances directly.

definition.value: An ordinal classification of the assessed magnitude of a security risk.
Risk requiring prioritized treatment because of substantial expected harm or exposure.
Risk requiring immediate action because of extreme expected harm or exposure.
Risk requiring planned treatment and continued monitoring.
Risk whose expected harm and exposure are limited.

A type of flaw, fault, or design condition in software, hardware, or system architecture that can enable vulnerabilities, reduce security assurance, or increase the likelihood of exploitable behavior.

scopeNote.value: This class provides a semantic representation of weakness types defined in the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE). It supports hierarchical relationships, abstraction levels, and mappings to related attack patterns, vulnerabilities, and security controls.

comment.undefined: Instances of stonework:Weakness may represent base weaknesses, variant weaknesses, or compound weaknesses. CWE identifiers (e.g., "CWE‑79") SHOULD be modeled using explicit properties rather than encoded in the class IRI. Descriptions and extended details SHOULD be referenced via citations rather than reproduced verbatim.

definition.value: An on-chain address that identifies a destination for value on a distributed ledger.

scopeNote.value: The address string is stonework:walletAddress. Attach a CryptoAddress to the wallet it identifies, a stonework:FinancialAccount, with stonework:hasIdentifier; the address's asset and network are then traversable through ^stonework:hasIdentifier/stonework:accountCurrency and stonework:blockchainNetwork. Sibling of stonework:EmailAddress and stonework:MACAddress.

definition.value: A systematic Process of inquiry, evidence collection, analysis, hypothesis testing, and conclusion to understand, attribute, or resolve security incidents, threats, anomalies, or other matters of interest.

scopeNote.value: Includes digital forensics, threat hunting, root cause analysis, and incident investigations. Links to Sightings, Evidence (via categorizedBy), Sensors, and produces Findings or updated Assessments.

definition.value: Any collection of Persons, Organizations, or other Groups that share a common purpose or identity but do not necessarily have formal legal structure.

scopeNote.value: Used for informal collectives, communities, ad-hoc teams, criminal syndicates, or loose alliances. More general than Organization. Can contain other Groups or Organizations.

definition.value: One of the classic phases of a money-laundering scheme — placement, layering, or integration — grouping the techniques that serve that phase's objective.

scopeNote.value: The illicit-finance counterpart of stonework:OffensiveTactic: a high-level objective that groups stonework:IllicitFinanceTechnique individuals via stonework:hasTechnique. A neutral structural slot; the three canonical individuals are supplied by frameworks/fatf.ttl.

definition.value: A plan specification describing how a threat could materialize against specific assets or missions — incorporating adversary intent, capability, opportunity, preconditions, attack path, and expected consequences.

scopeNote.value: A ThreatScenario is prescriptive and forward-looking: it specifies a potential sequence of adversary behaviors and environmental conditions rather than recording observed events. Used to guide defensive planning, risk assessment, and Playbook development. Distinct from stonework:Incident (an observed occurrence) and stonework:Threat (an abstract source of harm). Aligns with prov:Plan and P-Plan scenario specifications.

definition.value: A digital representation or persona of an Agent, inferred from one or more identifiers (email, phone, account, etc.). It may or may not be attributed to a known real-world Agent.

scopeNote.value: Useful when you observe identifiers without confirmed attribution. Can aggregate multiple Identifiers and later be linked to a real-worldAgent.

definition.value: Any concept, object, or resource that exists or operates within a cyber or sociotechnical domain.

scopeNote.value: One of two root classes in STONEWORK. Groups all persistent entities — Agents, Infrastructure, DigitalArtifacts, PhysicalArtifacts, Behaviors, IntelligenceProducts, SecurityConditions, RiskFactors, Countermeasures, and related classes. Aligns with BFO Continuant. The sibling root class CyberActivity covers happenings (Campaigns, Incidents, Operations, etc.).

definition.value: A discrete unit of data stored on a filesystem, identified by name, path, and cryptographic hash. Includes executable binaries, scripts, documents, archives, and other file types relevant to cyber threat analysis.

scopeNote.value: Linked to hash values via stonework:hasHash. A MalwareSample may be associated with its File representation. Framework-specific extensions (PE headers, NTFS streams, archive contents) are modeled at the framework layer.

definition.value: A flaw or weakness in software, hardware, firmware, or system architecture that can be exploited by a threat actor to compromise confidentiality, integrity, or availability.

scopeNote.value: Represents specific exploitable instances (e.g., CVE-identified vulnerabilities) rather than weakness classes — those are modeled as stonework:Weakness. A Vulnerability is linked to its root Weakness via stonework:hasWeakness, to affected products via stonework:affected, to its fix via stonework:fixedInProduct, and to exploiting malware or actors via stonework:exploits. Aligns with D3FEND Vulnerability and NVD CVE.

definition.value: A structured data source that provides indicators, intelligence, or enrichment data on a regular or continuous basis.

scopeNote.value: Examples: URLHaus, AlienVault OTX, Abuse.ch, commercial threat feeds, etc.

definition.value: A computing system, device, or endpoint (physical, virtual, container, or cloud instance) that can run processes, host files, and participate in networks.
A qualified, time-stamped metric value about a cyber entity, carrying its metric type, source provenance, and optional calculation-model version.

scopeNote.value: Use for values that change over time or differ by source, including EPSS probability, KEV membership, confidence, likelihood, risk scores, and normalized monetary valuations. A stonework:metricNormalizedValue observation records its output currency with stonework:valuationCurrency. Direct datatype properties remain convenience projections for consumers that need a single current value.

definition.value: A discrete, observable instance of malicious code — a specific binary, script, or executable artifact that can be identified by cryptographic hash, file characteristics, or behavioral signature.

scopeNote.value: Represents a concrete sample rather than an abstract family concept. A single MalwareFamily may have thousands of associated samples across versions, packers, and dropper variants. Samples are linked to their family via stonework:memberOfFamily and to their file representation via stonework:hasHash or a direct stonework:File association. Properties such as stonework:drops, stonework:downloads, and stonework:communicatesWith describe the behavior of this specific sample, not the family in general.

definition.value: The magnitude of harm, loss, or adverse effects that would result if a threat were realized and a compromise occurred, expressed in terms of mission, business, operational, or technical consequences.

scopeNote.value: Impact represents the severity of consequences associated with a compromise. It may include effects on confidentiality, integrity, availability, safety, mission success, financial loss, or reputational damage. Impact values may be qualitative or quantitative.

comment.undefined: Instances of stonework:Impact SHOULD specify the affected asset or mission, the type of consequence, and the severity level. Impact SHOULD be represented using explicit properties rather than encoded in class IRIs or labels.

definition.value: A classification of a threat actor's assessed technical sophistication.
The actor develops novel techniques or capabilities not commonly observed elsewhere.
The actor demonstrates deep expertise across multiple technical domains.
The actor can customize existing tools and execute moderately complex operations.
The actor can develop or adapt complex capabilities and conduct multi-stage operations.
The actor combines advanced capability with long-term planning and coordinated resourcing.
No meaningful technical sophistication has been demonstrated.
The actor relies primarily on basic or readily available capabilities.
A prescribed defensive method used to detect, prevent, or respond to adversary behavior within a target environment.

scopeNote.value: Aligns with MITRE D3FEND DefensiveTechnique. Framework-specific subclasses (e.g. d3fend:DefensiveTechnique) extend this class when D3FEND data is loaded.

definition.value: A euro-denominated credit transfer within the Single Euro Payments Area.
A firm that trades securities for its own account or on behalf of customers.
A government or state-sponsored actor conducting cyber operations for geopolitical objectives.
The outcome is assessed as plausible but not more likely than not.
A stored-value balance held with a non-financial merchant or platform, such as gift-card credit, marketplace store credit, or in-platform currency redeemable for goods.
Self-replicating malware that spreads across networks or systems without requiring user interaction or a host file to attach to.
Disclosure is not limited.
A licensed deposit-taking bank serving retail or corporate customers.
A non-human account used by a service, workload, or automated process.
Malware that replicates by inserting copies of itself into other executable files or documents, spreading when those files are executed or opened.
An individual with technical skills conducting intrusions, ranging from hobbyist to professional.
Malware that masquerades as legitimate security software to deceive users into paying for fake threat removal or granting elevated privileges.
A movement of value from one account to another.
The outcome is assessed as exceptional or highly unlikely.
A threat actor using cyber means to cause fear, disruption, or harm in support of extremist goals.
The actor can develop or adapt complex capabilities and conduct multi-stage operations.
A threat actor who executes operations on behalf of a directing or sponsoring entity.
Malware that conceals itself and other malicious software by subverting operating system or hypervisor mechanisms, typically to maintain privileged persistence.
A reusable collection of code, routines, or resources linked into applications or other software components, often a source of transitive vulnerabilities.
Malware that abuses the computational resources of an infected host, such as for cryptocurrency mining or proxying network traffic.
The incident is under active investigation or response.
A threat actor motivated by political, religious, or social beliefs; actions intended to advance or defend a particular worldview.
Impact involving direct or indirect monetary loss.
Malware that provides covert, persistent remote access to a compromised system, bypassing normal authentication.
Malware designed to conduct or participate in distributed denial-of-service attacks against target systems or networks.
Infrastructure used as an intermediate point for storing tools, payloads, or exfiltrated data during an operation.
The Hypothesis has not yet been tested against an actual result.
A transactional deposit account at a bank or credit union, used for routine payments and withdrawals.
Malware designed to irreversibly destroy data or render systems inoperable, typically used for sabotage or to obscure attacker activity.

Software permanently programmed into a hardware device, typically stored in non-volatile memory and providing low-level control of the device. Corresponds to CPE component type 'o' when used in embedded contexts.
An account managed within an enterprise identity domain.
A trained machine learning or AI model distributed as a deployable artifact, subject to threats such as model poisoning, extraction, inversion, and adversarial evasion.
Network routing and switching equipment, often targeted or co-opted by adversaries.
No meaningful technical sophistication has been demonstrated.
Resources typical of a small, informally organized group.
Risk whose expected harm and exposure are limited.
An account managed locally by a host or application.
A threat actor who is being forced to act against their will; actions taken under duress or threat.
The rule is expected to generate false positives frequently.
A likelihood or probability score on the 0.0–1.0 scale.
Limited disclosure, restricted to participants' organization and its clients.
An interbank credit transfer settled individually, such as Fedwire, CHAPS, or a cross-border SWIFT payment.
The actor can customize existing tools and execute moderately complex operations.
A threat actor seeking to assert superiority or control over a target, competitor, or adversary; establishing authority or influence.
Value added to an account from an external source.
Malware that records keystrokes on an infected system to capture credentials, sensitive data, or communications.
The actor relies primarily on basic or readily available capabilities.
A transfer made in consideration for goods, services, or an obligation.
The outcome is assessed as not expected to occur in most circumstances.
Resources comparable to those available to a national government.
A threat actor whose motivation is unknown, unclear, or inconsistent; actions that do not fit a clear pattern of intent.
A currency-normalized valuation of a monetary amount — for example the USD equivalent of a crypto transfer — at a stated observation time and exchange-rate source.
A threat actor seeking retaliation for a perceived wrong; actions motivated by grievance against a specific target.
An impact causing extraordinary or potentially irreversible harm.
A threat actor driven by curiosity, intellectual challenge, or the intrinsic satisfaction of successfully executing an attack.
Risk requiring prioritized treatment because of substantial expected harm or exposure.
An account with a payment service provider or e-money institution, such as a digital wallet or peer-to-peer payment balance.
Malware deployed on a web server that provides remote command execution via HTTP requests, enabling persistent access through the web application layer.
Impact involving potential harm to people or physical well-being.
An individual or loosely organized group conducting cyber crimes for personal financial benefit.
An account managed by a cloud service or identity provider.
Resources available to a single person.
Infrastructure used to store or distribute lists of targets for operations.
Infrastructure used to host or distribute malicious payloads.
A crypto-asset wallet whose on-chain keys are held by the accountholder, with no custodian.
An impact causing major operational, financial, or safety harm.
An account holding securities or other investment assets on behalf of the accountholder.
A national or supranational monetary authority.
The outcome is assessed as expected to occur in nearly all relevant circumstances.
An impact causing localized or readily recoverable harm.
Response work is complete and the incident has been formally closed.
A networked or cloud-hosted software capability consumed by other systems or users, such as a SaaS platform, API service, or managed infrastructure service.
A physical computing device, component, or peripheral. Corresponds to CPE component type 'h'.
Malware disguised as or bundled with legitimate software to deceive users into executing it, enabling a range of malicious payloads.
Malware that connects an infected host to a command-and-control network, enabling remote tasking as part of a botnet.
Malware whose primary function is to download and execute additional malicious payloads from a remote source.
An insider who causes harm unintentionally through negligence or error.
An interest-bearing deposit account with limited transactional use.
A threat actor who develops malicious code used in operations.
Malware that carries and installs one or more secondary payloads onto a target system, often unpacking them from within itself.
A batched account-to-account credit or debit transfer over an automated clearing house.
The malware type has not been determined or cannot be classified into a known category.
A threat actor who maintains and operates technical infrastructure during an operation.
A physical currency deposit, withdrawal, or hand-to-hand payment.
Risk requiring immediate action because of extreme expected harm or exposure.
A threat actor conducting cyber espionage to collect intelligence for a state or organization.
Risk requiring planned treatment and continued monitoring.
A toolkit that automates exploitation of client-side vulnerabilities to deliver malware, typically via drive-by download from compromised or malicious web pages.
A current or former employee, contractor, or partner acting maliciously due to grievance.
Infrastructure used to gather information about targets prior to an operation.
A business that exchanges, transfers, or custodies virtual assets for others — a crypto exchange, custodial wallet provider, or similar (the FATF VASP category).
Resources available to a coordinated operational team.
A software development kit providing tools, libraries, and APIs used to build applications for a specific platform or framework.
Malware that covertly monitors user activity, collects personal or sensitive information, and transmits it to a remote party.
An assertion that a specific pattern or set of Digital Artifacts is associated with malicious behavior, enabling detection, correlation, and response.

scopeNote.value: In STONEWORK, Indicators can be simple (single IOC like a hash or IP) or complex (full STIX patterns combining multiple artifacts and conditions).

definition.value: A CVSS base score on the 0.0–10.0 scale.
A numeric risk score calculated using a stated methodology or assessment model.
Malware that infects the boot sector or master boot record to load before the operating system, enabling deep persistence and defense evasion.
A member-owned cooperative deposit-taking institution.
A custodial crypto-asset balance held for a customer by an exchange or virtual asset service provider, controlled through the provider rather than by an on-chain key the customer holds.
A stored-value balance accessed through a prepaid or reloadable payment card, which may be issued without full identity verification.
Limited disclosure, restricted to the community.
A threat actor motivated by financial reward or material benefit for themselves.
Infrastructure used to obscure the origin of operations, such as VPNs, proxies, or Tor nodes.
A threat actor motivated primarily by notoriety, publicity, or the thrill of the attack.
Not for disclosure, restricted to participants only.
Software that automatically displays or downloads advertising material, often without user consent.
Impact involving loss of stakeholder trust or public standing.
The rule is expected to generate false positives infrequently.
Impact involving unauthorized disclosure of information.

A distributable unit of software published to a package registry (e.g. npm, PyPI, Maven, NuGet). The primary unit of supply chain attack surface — distinct from Library in that a package has its own versioning, signing, provenance chain, and registry identity.
A charge deducted by an institution, network, or ledger for processing a transaction.
The Hypothesis's predicted value did not match the actual value the predicted Variable was bound to.
A packaged, layered filesystem image used to instantiate containers. Subject to threats including image tampering, malicious base layers, and registry poisoning.
A software application designed to perform specific tasks for end users or other systems. Corresponds to CPE component type 'a'.
A threat actor motivated by political, social, or ideological causes, using cyber means to advance their agenda.
A company that processes payment card or account-to-account transactions between parties.
An account one financial institution holds at another to settle cross-border or cross-institution payments on behalf of its customers.
Malware that encrypts or locks victim data or systems and demands payment for restoration of access.
The incident has been declared and remains unresolved.
Infrastructure used as a destination or relay for stolen data.
A threat actor responsible for designing and building the technical infrastructure supporting operations.
A threat actor seeking to benefit their organization, nation-state, or group through espionage, competitive intelligence, or strategic advantage.
Value removed from an account to an external destination, including cash-out.
A 0–100 score expressing confidence in an assertion or expected outcome.
An end-user computing device, typically a target or pivot point in an operation.
A conversion of value from one currency to another, including fiat-to-crypto and crypto-to-crypto swaps.
An organized criminal group conducting cyber operations for financial gain.
The outcome is assessed as more likely than not to occur.
An EPSS probability score on the 0.0–1.0 scale.
A transfer of a crypto asset recorded on a distributed ledger.
Impact affecting timely and reliable access to systems or information.
A network of compromised systems under adversary control, used to execute distributed attacks or other operations.
A business that transmits or converts money, including money transmitters, currency exchangers, and check cashers.
Malware that periodically or continuously captures screenshots of the victim's display and exfiltrates them to an attacker.
Impact involving unauthorized alteration or loss of trustworthiness.
Malware providing covert remote control of an infected host, typically including capabilities such as file access, screen capture, keylogging, and command execution.
A payment made with a credit, debit, or prepaid payment card.
A commercial entity conducting cyber espionage or sabotage against business rivals.
Defensive infrastructure that filters and monitors network traffic.
Limited disclosure, restricted to participants' organization.
A threat actor seeking fame, recognition, or infamy; actions intended to demonstrate capability or gain public public attention.
A prepaid negotiable instrument issued by a bank or money services business.
Infrastructure used to communicate with and issue commands to compromised systems.
Infrastructure used to amplify attack traffic, such as DNS or NTP amplification servers.
The rule is expected to generate false positives at a moderate frequency.
An impact causing material but manageable harm.
The actor demonstrates deep expertise across multiple technical domains.
The balance of a financial account at a point in time, in a stated currency.
A threat actor who funds or otherwise enables operations without direct participation.
A dated boolean observation of whether a vulnerability appears in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.
Resources assembled temporarily for a competition or challenge.
The incident's spread or immediate harmful activity has been stopped.
The actor develops novel techniques or capabilities not commonly observed elsewhere.
A threat actor who plans and directs operations without necessarily executing them.
The Hypothesis's predicted value matched the actual value the predicted Variable was bound to.
Resources available to a sustained formal organization.
The actor combines advanced capability with long-term planning and coordinated resourcing.
Material or information offered to support or refute a claim, typically within an investigation or legal context.

scopeNote.value: This is a reusable category instance. It is *not* a class. Use stonework:categorizedBy to assert that something is evidence in a given context.

definition.value: A threat actor who did not have intent to cause harm; unintentional or inadvertent actions that result in a security incident.
Infrastructure used to conduct phishing campaigns, including fake login pages or malicious email servers.
System software that manages hardware resources and provides common services for application software. Corresponds to CPE component type 'o'.
An autonomous or semi-autonomous system driven by AI/ML that can act, make decisions, or be attributed responsibility in a cyber or sociotechnical context.

scopeNote.value: Covers both offensive uses (AI-assisted or autonomous threat actors) and defensive uses (AI-driven detection, response, or hunting systems). Distinct from Tool — an AIAgent has a degree of autonomous decision-making rather than being a passively invoked artifact.

definition.value: A classification of a Hypothesis's position in the confirm/refute lifecycle.

scopeNote.value: Applied via stonework:hasHypothesisStatus to Hypothesis individuals. Named individuals: pending (not yet tested), confirmed (actual result matched the prediction), refuted (actual result did not match the prediction).

definition.value: The Hypothesis's predicted value matched the actual value the predicted Variable was bound to.
The Hypothesis's predicted value did not match the actual value the predicted Variable was bound to.
The Hypothesis has not yet been tested against an actual result.

An intelligence assertion that a pattern — atomic, expression-based, or behavioral — when matched in an observed environment, indicates the presence of threat activity attributable to a specific adversary behavior, malware, or campaign.

scopeNote.value: The central concept in operational CTI. The term is used by the community in three overlapping senses, all of which stonework:Indicator covers: (1) IOC sense — an atomic observable (IP address, domain, file hash, URL) that has been assessed as malicious or suspicious and tagged for detection; in STONEWORK the underlying observable is the SCO (stonework:IPAddress, stonework:Domain, stonework:Hash), and the Indicator wraps it with the assertion, confidence, and validity window. (2) Pattern sense — a STIX patterning expression over one or more SCOs (e.g., [ipv4-addr:value = ‘198.51.100.0/24’]). (3) Behavioral sense — a multi-step or TTPs-based pattern asserting that an observed sequence of behaviors indicates a technique or campaign. Distinct from stonework:DetectionRule: an Indicator is the intelligence claim (‘look for this’); a DetectionRule is the operational artifact that implements the check (‘here is the Sigma/Snort/YARA rule that looks for it’). Indicators are produced by threat intelligence analysts and consumed by detection pipelines; DetectionRules are deployed in SIEMs, EDRs, and network sensors. Corresponds to STIX 2.1 Indicator SDO. Use stonework:indicates to link an Indicator to the AttackPattern, Malware, Campaign, or ThreatActor it asserts.

definition.value: An analyst's epistemological stance on the correctness or credibility of information asserted in another intelligence object.

scopeNote.value: Sibling to stonework:Assessment under IntelligenceProduct. Where Assessment evaluates risk or impact, Opinion evaluates the reliability or accuracy of existing intelligence — e.g., 'I disagree with this threat score' or 'I believe this indicator attribution is incorrect'. Corresponds to STIX 2.1 Opinion SDO. The opinion value (strongly-agree to strongly-disagree) and explanation are captured via stones: properties.

definition.value: Defines a data handling marking used to restrict or label how data can be shared or handled, such as TLP markings. Referenced by object_marking_refs or granular_markings.
Limited disclosure, restricted to participants' organization and its clients.
Limited disclosure, restricted to the community.
Limited disclosure, restricted to participants' organization.
Disclosure is not limited.
Not for disclosure, restricted to participants only.
A sovereign state or top-level administrative entity recognized internationally.
Represents a user group on a system or service, including local OS groups, cloud groups, and social media groups.
Structured source references used to record the origin and trustworthiness of data and relationships.

scopeNote.value: Includes Feeds, Publications, and URL References.

definition.value: Represents a network domain name. Can reference the IP addresses it resolves to.
A deployed system, appliance, agent, or network tap that collects data about digital artifacts, network activity, or adversary behavior for detection and investigation purposes.

scopeNote.value: Applies DetectionRules via stonework:usesRule. May be a software agent, physical appliance, virtual instance, or network sensor. Examples: IDS/IPS, SIEM collector, endpoint agent, network tap, honeypot, vulnerability scanner. An AI-driven sensor that crosses into autonomous decision-making may be additionally typed as stonework:AIAgent. Aligns with D3FEND Sensor. Inspired by SOSA sosa:Sensor — compatible in concept but does not formally import the SOSA ontology. Produces stonework:SecurityObservation instances via stonework:madeBySensor.

definition.value: A cryptocurrency, stablecoin, or other token that serves as a unit of value on a distributed ledger.

scopeNote.value: Instances are the assets themselves (e.g. Bitcoin, Ether, a specific ERC-20 token) — not wallets, addresses, or holdings. A wallet is modeled as a stonework:FinancialAccount and its address as a stonework:CryptoAddress; an amount of a crypto asset is a stonework:MonetaryAmount whose stonework:currency is the CryptoAsset. The same nominal token issued on multiple ledgers is modeled as distinct individuals distinguished by stonework:blockchainNetwork. 'Virtual asset' is the FATF term; a service that custodies or exchanges them is a virtual asset service provider (stonework:FinancialInstitution categorized accordingly).

definition.value: A collection of threat intelligence focused on one or more topics, such as a description of a threat actor, malware, or attack technique.
A single, individually addressable unit of action within a Behavior that models a multi-step process, such as a Procedure, Playbook, ThreatScenario, or Control.

scopeNote.value: A Step is itself a Behavior — a plan specification for a sub-action, not its execution — consistent with p-plan:Step subclassing prov:Plan rather than prov:Activity. Because Step is a Behavior, a Step MAY itself decompose into further Steps via stonework:hasStep, supporting nested sub-procedures (e.g. a Kill Chain phase decomposing into candidate technique attempts) without a separate composite class. The activity that executes a Step is a stonework:CyberActivity; it links back to the Step it realizes via stonework:correspondsToStep.

definition.value: A technique performed within or against cyberspace, encompassing both offensive and defensive cyber operations.

scopeNote.value: Mirrors D3FEND's CyberTechnique class. Subclassed by stonework:AttackTechnique (offensive) and stonework:DefendTechnique (defensive), enabling a single property chain to span both ATT&CK and D3FEND individuals.

definition.value: A prescribed method for disguising the origin, ownership, or destination of illicitly obtained funds, or for moving value while evading financial controls.

scopeNote.value: Covers money-laundering typologies and the adjacent methods of terrorist financing, sanctions evasion, and financial fraud. A neutral structural slot: STONEWORK defines the class but not its individuals. A starter set of FATF-derived typology individuals is supplied by the optional frameworks/fatf.ttl module; other bodies' typology sets can populate the same class. Link an exhibiting stonework:FinancialTransaction or stonework:CyberActivityCluster with stonework:hasBehavior. Because the class sits under stonework:Technique, a concrete laundering chain can later be modeled as a stonework:Procedure that stonework:implements a typology, with no rework.

definition.value: A structured or semi-structured record of events, actions, or state changes generated by a system, application, or network component over time.

scopeNote.value: Logs are primary data sources for detection, investigation, and threat hunting. Examples include system event logs, authentication logs, DNS query logs, firewall logs, and application logs. Distinct from NetworkTraffic (which captures raw packet data) and from Event (which represents a parsed, security-relevant occurrence derived from log data).

definition.value: A classification of a product by its primary functional category within a system or architecture.

scopeNote.value: Applied via stonework:hasProductType to Product individuals. Aligns with CPE component type designations. A product may have more than one type (e.g. an embedded OS is both firmware and operating-system).

definition.value: A software application designed to perform specific tasks for end users or other systems. Corresponds to CPE component type 'a'.
A networked or cloud-hosted software capability consumed by other systems or users, such as a SaaS platform, API service, or managed infrastructure service.
A physical computing device, component, or peripheral. Corresponds to CPE component type 'h'.

Software permanently programmed into a hardware device, typically stored in non-volatile memory and providing low-level control of the device. Corresponds to CPE component type 'o' when used in embedded contexts.

A distributable unit of software published to a package registry (e.g. npm, PyPI, Maven, NuGet). The primary unit of supply chain attack surface — distinct from Library in that a package has its own versioning, signing, provenance chain, and registry identity.
A trained machine learning or AI model distributed as a deployable artifact, subject to threats such as model poisoning, extraction, inversion, and adversarial evasion.
A software development kit providing tools, libraries, and APIs used to build applications for a specific platform or framework.
A reusable collection of code, routines, or resources linked into applications or other software components, often a source of transitive vulnerabilities.
A packaged, layered filesystem image used to instantiate containers. Subject to threats including image tampering, malicious base layers, and registry poisoning.
System software that manages hardware resources and provides common services for application software. Corresponds to CPE component type 'o'.
A captured or observed network traffic flow between source and destination endpoints, including protocol, ports, payload characteristics, and timing.

scopeNote.value: Distinct from stonework:Log (which captures parsed event records) and stonework:Event (a security-relevant occurrence). NetworkTraffic is the raw flow artifact. May carry indicators such as user-agent strings, URI patterns, or certificate fingerprints observable in transit.

definition.value: A structured intelligence product that asserts shared context among a set of referenced cyber threat intelligence entities.

scopeNote.value: Use when related objects need to be collected without the narrative and publication semantics of a Report. Corresponds to the STIX 2.1 Grouping SDO.

definition.value: A concrete, Step-decomposed sequence of actions that implements a Control in a specific operational context.

scopeNote.value: Mirrors the Technique/Procedure split on the defensive side: stonework:Control is the abstract prescribed safeguard (a catalog entry, e.g. NIST AC-2 or a CIS control); ControlPlan is its concrete implementation as a Step sequence, linked back via stonework:implements. A ControlPlan is typically invoked from within a Playbook or DetectionPlan by a Step that stonework:implements it.

definition.value: An ordinal classification of the assessed likelihood that a security outcome will occur.
The outcome is assessed as expected to occur in nearly all relevant circumstances.
The outcome is assessed as more likely than not to occur.
The outcome is assessed as not expected to occur in most circumstances.
The outcome is assessed as exceptional or highly unlikely.
The outcome is assessed as plausible but not more likely than not.
A structured, machine-readable rule designed to detect malicious or suspicious activity, techniques, or indicators. It may be signature-based, behavioral, correlation-based, or analytic.

scopeNote.value: Encompasses pattern-matching signatures (YARA, Snort, Suricata), behavioral rules (Sigma), SIEM correlation logic, and analytic detections. Signature is a subclass for content-centric, indicator-matching rules.

definition.value: A classification of a user account by its authentication or deployment context.
An account managed by a cloud service or identity provider.
An account managed within an enterprise identity domain.
An account managed locally by a host or application.
A non-human account used by a service, workload, or automated process.
A broad division or category of economic activity, infrastructure, or society used for classification and targeting purposes.

scopeNote.value: Can represent both commercial industries and critical infrastructure sectors (e.g., from CISA or NIST frameworks).

definition.value: A significant adverse event or series of related events that has caused, or has the potential to cause, harm to an organization’s operations, assets, or people.

scopeNote.value: Distinguished from stonework:Event (a raw, unassessed occurrence) by the presence of human or automated triage declaring significance and adversity. An Incident may aggregate multiple Events, involve one or more Campaigns, and trigger Investigation and Playbook execution.

definition.value: A formal, machine-readable inventory of VersionedProduct components that constitute a software artifact or system, expressed in a standard format such as CycloneDX or SPDX.

scopeNote.value: SoftwareBillOfMaterials is a native STONEWORK class — not a subclass of any STIX domain object, as STIX 2.1 has no SBOM concept. Instances correspond to SBOM documents; format provenance (CycloneDX 1.6, SPDX 2.3, etc.) is expressed via stonework:bomFormat.

comment.en: An SBOM asserts that specific VersionedProduct instances are components of a containing artifact. Component entries are represented as stonework:BomEntry instances linked via stonework:hasBomEntry.

definition.value: A systematic examination of a cyber entity, artifact, or event that produces structured findings about its nature, behavior, or properties.

scopeNote.value: Sibling to stonework:Assessment under IntelligenceProduct. Where Assessment answers 'how bad/likely/risky?', Analysis answers 'what is it and what does it do?' Superclass for domain-specific analyses such as MalwareAnalysis. Aligns with STIX MalwareAnalysis SDO at the subclass level.

definition.value: An ordinal classification of the magnitude of a security impact.
An impact causing major operational, financial, or safety harm.
An impact causing localized or readily recoverable harm.
An impact causing material but manageable harm.
An impact causing extraordinary or potentially irreversible harm.
A named phase within a kill chain or attack lifecycle framework used to categorize the stage of an offensive or defensive operation.

scopeNote.value: Applies to both offensive frameworks (Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain, MITRE ATT&CK) and defensive lifecycle models. Used to tag AttackTechniques, Procedures, or Events with their operational phase.

definition.value: Any discrete digital object or content entity that can be observed, transmitted, stored, or acted upon in a cyber environment.

scopeNote.value: Includes files, hashes, malware samples, network traffic captures, and other content-bearing items. Aligns with D3FEND DigitalArtifact concepts. Sibling of stonework:PhysicalArtifact.

definition.value: A high‑level objective or strategic goal that groups related techniques by the purpose they serve during an operation.

scopeNote.value: Superclass for OffensiveTactic and DefensiveTactic. Tactics represent the strategic intent behind behavior — gaining initial access, exfiltrating data, or hardening a system. They serve as conceptual categories for techniques.

comment.undefined: Instances of stonework:Tactic SHOULD correspond to high‑level adversary goals. Techniques are typically modeled as children or members of a tactic.

definition.value: A pattern of actions or methods characteristic of an entity, particularly adversaries.

scopeNote.value: Groups TTP-related classes: Tactic, Technique (and subclasses), and Procedure. In BFO terms, Behaviors are GenericallyDependentContinuants — specifications or patterns describing how actions are carried out. The execution of a Technique is a CyberActivity; the Technique itself is a Behavior. Aligns with IAO PlanSpecification.

definition.value: The reason or driving force behind an adversary's decision to conduct an attack or operation.

scopeNote.value: Applied via stonework:categorizedBy to ThreatActor, Campaign, or Operation individuals. Named individuals cover the STIX 2.1 attack-motivation open vocabulary. Custom motivations may be added as additional individuals.

definition.value: A threat actor motivated by political, religious, or social beliefs; actions intended to advance or defend a particular worldview.
A threat actor whose motivation is unknown, unclear, or inconsistent; actions that do not fit a clear pattern of intent.
A threat actor seeking to benefit their organization, nation-state, or group through espionage, competitive intelligence, or strategic advantage.
A threat actor seeking to assert superiority or control over a target, competitor, or adversary; establishing authority or influence.
A threat actor seeking retaliation for a perceived wrong; actions motivated by grievance against a specific target.
A threat actor seeking fame, recognition, or infamy; actions intended to demonstrate capability or gain public public attention.
A threat actor motivated by financial reward or material benefit for themselves.
A threat actor who did not have intent to cause harm; unintentional or inadvertent actions that result in a security incident.
A threat actor driven by curiosity, intellectual challenge, or the intrinsic satisfaction of successfully executing an attack.
A threat actor who is being forced to act against their will; actions taken under duress or threat.
A collective, organization, or coordinated set of individuals operating with common intent to conduct adversarial cyber activities.

scopeNote.value: Covers nation-state units, cybercriminal organizations, hacktivist collectives, and other named adversary groups. Industry names such as APT20 or APT29 are often used for both a tracked body of activity and the presumed group behind it. Model the activity as a separate stonework:CyberActivityCluster and link it to the ThreatActorGroup with stonework:attributedTo when supported. MITRE ATT&CK serializes tracked Groups as STIX intrusion-set objects; that source representation alone does not establish that the activity cluster and responsible group are the same entity. Distinguished from stonework:ThreatActorIndividual, which represents a single human actor.

definition.value: A classification of a financial institution by its regulatory form and the service it provides.
A national or supranational monetary authority.
A company that processes payment card or account-to-account transactions between parties.
A firm that trades securities for its own account or on behalf of customers.
A member-owned cooperative deposit-taking institution.
A business that exchanges, transfers, or custodies virtual assets for others — a crypto exchange, custodial wallet provider, or similar (the FATF VASP category).
A business that transmits or converts money, including money transmitters, currency exchangers, and check cashers.
A licensed deposit-taking bank serving retail or corporate customers.
A controlled vocabulary of operators used to compare a Variable's bound value against a threshold in a Transition guard.

scopeNote.value: Individuals are stonework:Equals, stonework:NotEquals, stonework:LessThan, stonework:LessThanOrEqual, stonework:GreaterThan, and stonework:GreaterThanOrEqual. Referenced by stonework:guardOperator; omitting an operator on a guard defaults to Equals semantics.

definition.value: The guardVariable's bound value is greater than guardLiteralValue.
The guardVariable's bound value does not equal guardLiteralValue.
The guardVariable's bound value is less than or equal to guardLiteralValue.
The guardVariable's bound value is greater than or equal to guardLiteralValue.
The guardVariable's bound value equals guardLiteralValue.
The guardVariable's bound value is less than guardLiteralValue.
An ordinal classification of the expected false-positive frequency of a detection rule.
The rule is expected to generate false positives infrequently.
The rule is expected to generate false positives at a moderate frequency.
The rule is expected to generate false positives frequently.
Represents an Autonomous System (AS), a collection of IP routing prefixes under the control of a single administrative entity, identified by its AS number.
A qualified record assigning a Role to an entity within a particular campaign, operation, organization, or other context.

scopeNote.value: Create separate assignments when the same entity plays different roles in different contexts or time intervals. The assignment can infer the context-free stonework:playsRole projection through the declared property chain.

definition.value: A classification of the organizational resources available to a threat actor.
Resources assembled temporarily for a competition or challenge.
Resources comparable to those available to a national government.
Resources available to a single person.
Resources available to a sustained formal organization.
Resources available to a coordinated operational team.
Resources typical of a small, informally organized group.
A prescribed analytical method used to process, evaluate, or reason over data to produce intelligence, detections, or assessments.

scopeNote.value: Covers structured analytic techniques (e.g., analysis of competing hypotheses, kill chain analysis, diamond model analysis) and computational analytic methods (e.g., clustering, anomaly detection). Distinct from DetectionRule — an AnalyticTechnique describes the method; a DetectionRule is a deployable artifact implementing it.

definition.value: A running or terminated process instance on a host, identified by PID, executable path, command line, parent process, and associated user account.

scopeNote.value: Represents low-level OS process objects observed during execution — distinct from stonework:Process (enterprise-level workflows). Mutex objects created by a process are linked as stonework:Mutex individuals. Corresponds to STIX 2.1 Process SCO.

definition.value: A discrete material object relevant to cyber operations — a device, appliance, plant component, or other physical artifact that can be observed, located, or acted upon.

scopeNote.value: Sibling of stonework:DigitalArtifact. Covers ICS and OT assets such as PLCs, RTUs, safety systems, and HMIs, as well as other tangible devices in a cyber-physical environment. An ICS device that runs processes and participates in networks may also be typed as stonework:Host. Distinct from stonework:Infrastructure, which groups resources used to conduct cyber operations.

definition.value: A software object intended to perform malicious functions within, or on behalf of, a threat actor. Encompasses both abstract family-level concepts and concrete specimen-level artifacts.

scopeNote.value: Parent class for stonework:MalwareFamily (STIX is_family=true) and stonework:MalwareSample (STIX is_family=false). Corresponds to the STIX 2.1 malware SDO. Use stonework:categorizedBy to assert behavioral type (e.g., stonework:Ransomware). Use stonework:hasArtifact to link a sample to its captured binary.

definition.value: A marking application that assigns a data-handling marking to selected fields or portions of another cyber entity.

scopeNote.value: Represents the structural application of a marking, including its selectors and referenced marking definition. It is distinct from a stonework:Markings category value, which expresses the handling designation itself.

definition.value: A single component entry within a Software Bill of Materials, asserting that a specific VersionedProduct is included in the artifact or system described by the SBOM.

scopeNote.value: An SBOM import creates one BomEntry per declared component. The BomEntry IRI is scoped to the SBOM (e.g. <sbom-iri/entry/<component-ref>>). Multiple BomEntry instances across different SBOMs may reference the same VersionedProduct via stonework:installationOf.

comment.en: BomEntry is the STONEWORK representation of a CycloneDX component element or SPDX package entry. It links a VersionedProduct into the context of a particular SBOM document via stonework:installationOf, and may carry component-specific metadata (PURL, license, hash, component type) that does not belong on the VersionedProduct itself.

definition.value: Any control, mitigation, or safeguard applied to protect against, reduce, or respond to security risks.

scopeNote.value: Includes Controls, Mitigations, CoursesOfAction, and DetectionRules. The two primary branches are preventive/reactive measures (Mitigation, CourseOfAction, Control) and detection logic (DetectionRule, Signature). A Countermeasure describes the safeguard or procedure; the deployed mechanism that can apply it is a stonework:SecurityActuator, and a particular application is a stonework:SecurityActuation.

definition.value: A classification of the instrument or rail used to move value in a financial transaction.
A batched account-to-account credit or debit transfer over an automated clearing house.
A euro-denominated credit transfer within the Single Euro Payments Area.
A physical currency deposit, withdrawal, or hand-to-hand payment.
An interbank credit transfer settled individually, such as Fedwire, CHAPS, or a cross-border SWIFT payment.
A payment made with a credit, debit, or prepaid payment card.
A transfer of a crypto asset recorded on a distributed ledger.
A prepaid negotiable instrument issued by a bank or money services business.
A sub-national territorial division such as a state, province, region, or governorate.
A single human individual.

scopeNote.value: Represents real named people (e.g. employees, threat actors, researchers). Does not include legal entities or groups. Corresponds to STIX Identity with identity_class = 'individual'.

definition.value: A movement of economic value from one financial account to another, occurring over a definite period and optionally attributed to the agents responsible for initiating it.

scopeNote.value: An occurrent: it starts and settles at a time (stonework:startedAtTime and stonework:endedAtTime), is attributed with stonework:attributedTo, and can be sighted, investigated, and grouped into a stonework:CyberActivityCluster. Originator and beneficiary are given by stonework:originatorAccount and stonework:beneficiaryAccount; correspondent hops by stonework:intermediaryAccount. The transferred value is a stonework:MonetaryAmount via stonework:hasMonetaryValue. Use stonework:originatorMonetaryValue and stonework:beneficiaryMonetaryValue when the debited input and credited output differ, as in a currency exchange. Flat stonework:transactionAmount and stonework:transactionCurrency are convenience projections only for a single-denomination transfer. A blockchain transaction is a FinancialTransaction whose accounts are crypto wallets. Divergent source records of one economic event are handled through stonework:hasProvenance and stonework:Sighting rather than a distinct record class. Use stonework:hasBehavior to link a transaction, or a cluster of them, to a stonework:IllicitFinanceTechnique it exhibits. Use stonework:fundsActivity only when the transaction finances an activity; use stonework:respondsToActivity when a transaction occurs in response to an activity, such as a victim's ransom payment.

definition.value: A directed edge between two Steps within the same parent Behavior's Step graph, representing progression from one Step to the next.

scopeNote.value: Unconditioned, a Transition expresses plain sequence — an alternative to stonework:precededByStep for the same purpose, used when a Step has more than one possible successor and the edges themselves need to be individually referenceable. When a Transition's stonework:toStep targets a Step already reached earlier in the same graph, it expresses a loop back-edge; looping is not a separate construct. Conditional branching is expressed with the guard properties stonework:guardVariable (the Variable tested), stonework:guardType (a class the bound value must be an instance of) or stonework:guardLiteralValue (a scalar it must equal), and stonework:guardOperator (the comparison; omitting it defaults to equality). The Transition fires when its guard holds against the from-Step's bound Variable.

definition.value: Represents a geographic location. May be as specific as a latitude/longitude coordinate or as broad as a continent. At least one of region, country, or latitude/longitude must be provided.

scopeNote.value: STONEWORK Location is a STIX-style geographic designator, not a BFO Site of occupancy. The BFO adapter maps it to an information content entity that denotes a place.

definition.value: A structured, falsifiable prediction about the value a Variable will resolve to once the Behavior or Step declaring that Variable executes.

scopeNote.value: Formalizes the anticipated side of the Variable lifecycle described in stonework:Variable's scopeNote: a Hypothesis names, in advance, the value an output Variable is predicted to be bound to. Linked to the Variable it predicts via stonework:predictsVariable, and to the prediction itself via stonework:predictedType (a class, the common case — mirrors stonework:guardType), stonework:predictedValue (a specific individual), or stonework:predictedLiteral (a scalar) — mirroring stonework:boundTo/stonework:boundToLiteral on the actual-result side. A Transition's guard properties, which test a Variable's actual bound value, implicitly test agreement with whichever Hypothesis predicted that Variable — confirming it if they match, refuting it otherwise. May attach at any level of a Step/Plan decomposition, since stonework:Step is itself a stonework:Behavior.

definition.value: A formal or semi-formal structured entity such as a company, government agency, non-profit, military unit, or consortium with defined boundaries and usually legal identity.

scopeNote.value: Corresponds to STIX Identity with identity_class = 'organization'. Includes corporations, government bodies, NGOs, universities, etc. Distinguished from Group by having more persistent structure, roles, and often legal standing.

definition.value: A structured digital document binding a public key to an identity, issued and signed by a certificate authority. Used for authentication, encryption, and trust establishment in networked systems.

scopeNote.value: Primarily represents X.509 certificates. May be used to cluster infrastructure sharing the same certificate or to link observed TLS/SSL artifacts to their issuing authority. Referenced by stonework:sharesCertificate on Infrastructure. Represent certificate fingerprints through stonework:hasHash and a stonework:Hash individual rather than algorithm-specific fingerprint literals.

definition.value: An analytically identified aggregate of cyber activities grouped because available evidence suggests a common source, mechanism, or operational thread.

scopeNote.value: A CyberActivityCluster is unified by analytic correlation rather than the objective and time period of a Campaign, the unified command or intent of an Operation, the execution sequence of a Process, or the inquiry purpose of an Investigation. It does not require a known objective, responsible Agent, precise boundaries, or a conclusion that the activity is adversarial. It denotes the body of activity believed to be related, not the intelligence artifact recording that judgment; use stonework:Grouping, stonework:Report, or stonework:Assessment for the artifact. Only CyberActivity instances are members through stonework:memberOfActivityCluster and stonework:hasMemberActivity; relate tools, malware, infrastructure, and responsible participants through their specific relationships. The STIX adapter maps its narrower intrusion-set source class to CyberActivityCluster.

definition.value: Represents a Uniform Resource Identifier conforming to RFC 3986.
A quantity of money: a decimal magnitude paired with the currency that denominates it.

scopeNote.value: Reified so magnitude and currency always travel together, mirroring how stonework:Hash pairs algorithm and digest. Attached to a transaction, account, impact, or demand with stonework:hasMonetaryValue or a monetary-value role subproperty. The magnitude is stonework:amount and the unit is stonework:currency. A currency-normalized valuation of the same amount, for example its USD equivalent at a stated time and rate source, is a stonework:MetricObservation on this amount with stonework:valuationCurrency identifying the output currency.

definition.value: A reusable, prescribed method for achieving an objective, which may be instantiated as a concrete execution by an actor or system.

scopeNote.value: A method specification, not a plan: a Technique describes an approach ('access credential material in LSASS process memory') without prescribing an ordered, branched sequence of steps. Concrete step structure appears one level down, in a stonework:Procedure that realizes the Technique, or in a stonework:Playbook / stonework:OperationPlan that orchestrates several. An execution links to the Technique it performs directly with stonework:executionOf — no Procedure, Plan, or Step is required for the lightweight case. Technique is intentionally not a subclass of stones:AttackPattern: attack patterns such as CAPEC are abstract taxonomy entries, while Techniques are operationalized methods closer to execution. See stonework:CyberTechnique, stonework:AttackTechnique, stonework:DefendTechnique, and docs/technique-modeling.md.
